response:
The veil-moth is a slow, luminous grazer of the tidally locked world Veyr, where one hemisphere is forever day and the other forever night, and life crowds the narrow twilight ring between them.

It is roughly the size of a small horse, but nothing about its shape reads as equine. The body is a low, flattened oval, about three meters long, sheathed in a flexible shell of interlocking plates the color of wet slate. The plates are not rigid armor so much as a living mosaic: each one can lift a few millimeters, and the gaps between them vent a pale vapor that smells, to a human nose, faintly of crushed mint and ozone. Beneath the shell, the flesh is cool and dense, more like chilled wax than muscle.

What looks at first like wings are four broad membranes stretched between long, jointed spars that rise from the creature’s back. They are not for flight. In the perpetual dusk they hang half-open, catching the faint blue-white light of Veyr’s parent star as it skims the horizon, and also the infrared glow of the warm rocks underfoot. The membranes are threaded with branching channels that carry a clear, mildly conductive fluid. When the veil-moth feeds, those channels brighten, and the whole canopy pulses in slow, uneven waves of blue-green light—communication as much as digestion, visible for kilometers across the plain.

Its face is a soft, puckered disk set low on the front of the shell, ringed by short sensory tendrils. It has no eyes in the usual sense. Instead, the tendrils and the underside of the membranes are studded with pits that read heat, vibration, and the chemical smear left by other veil-moths. It “sees” the world as overlapping maps of warmth, motion, and scent. A standing stone and a sleeping animal feel different not because of shape, but because one is quiet and cooling and the other is a knot of metabolic heat.

Feeding is a slow affair. The veil-moth lowers itself onto mats of black, rubbery ground-lichen that grow only in the twilight band. A slit opens along the belly, and a carpet of fine, glasslike filaments unrolls onto the mat. The filaments do not tear the lichen; they leach sugars and mineral salts through its surface, leaving pale, drained patches that regrow over weeks. While it feeds, the canopy membranes tilt to track the horizon-glow, and a low hum—barely audible, more felt in the chest than heard—rolls out across the rock. Other veil-moths answer with their own hums, and the plain fills with a staggered, tidal chorus.

It moves on six thick, pad-footed limbs arranged in two staggered rows. The pads are sticky when pressed and dry when lifted, so it can cross glazed ice and slick basalt without slipping. It never runs. Startled, it simply drops flat, seals its vents, and dims its membranes until it looks like another slab of stone. Predators on Veyr are few and mostly aerial—knife-winged things that hunt by the heat of exposed flesh—and a sealed veil-moth is a poor target: cold shell, no scent, no glow.

Reproduction is communal and oddly civic. Once every few local years, dozens gather in a shallow basin where warm groundwater seeps up through the lichen. They interlock the edges of their membranes, forming a low, glowing tent, and exchange packets of genetic material through the same belly filaments they use to feed. Weeks later, each adult extrudes a clutch of pebble-sized cysts into the damp mat. The cysts are not eggs in any simple sense; they are dormant kernels that wait for a rare alignment of warmth and mineral bloom before cracking open into thumb-sized juveniles, already glowing faintly, already grazing.

Old veil-moths accumulate mineral rims along the edges of their plates, pale as frost. The oldest become almost white, their membranes thin and slow to light, and they tend to linger near the basins where the young emerge—not guarding them, exactly, but lending the heat of their bodies and the steady pulse of their hum, a landmark the hatchlings can follow until their own senses settle.

In the long dusk of Veyr, a feeding herd looks less like animals than like a scatter of dim lanterns breathing in unison, each one a slow, stone-colored life that drinks light at the edge of a sun that never sets and never rises.

The hind pair are longer, digitigrade, and end in broad pads that can splay like snowshoes across the crust of dried algal mats. To a human ear it registers less as noise than as a pressure behind the sternum, a feeling that something large and patient is nearby and would prefer not to be crowded.

The glasslung lives on the windward cliffs of Vesh, a tidally locked world whose dayside is a slow kiln of mineral plains and whose nightside is a black ocean of frost. It never crosses the terminator. It keeps to the twilight band, where the air is thick enough to breathe and the light is a permanent, copper dusk.

It is roughly the size of a horse, but nothing about it suggests a horse once you look twice. The body is a low, ribbed oval of translucent cartilage, like a lung made visible. Through the walls you can see slow pulses of pale fluid moving in loops—no single heart, just a network of contractile vessels that squeeze in waves. Embedded in that fluid are thousands of mineral grains the creature has swallowed and sorted: iron flakes, silica beads, a few rare crystals that catch the dusk and throw tiny green sparks inward. Those grains are ballast, memory, and skeleton all at once. When the glasslung needs to climb, it shifts the heavier grains forward; when it wants to drift on an updraft, it lets them settle aft and the body lifts a hand’s width off the rock.

There are no legs. Along the underside run six flexible keels of the same glassy tissue, edged with a living sandpaper of microscopic hooks. They grip basalt the way a gecko grips glass, then release in sequence so the creature seems to pour uphill. On the flanks, two long fans unfurl—not wings exactly, more like sheets of stiffened mucus veined with dark filaments. They taste the wind. Each filament is a chemoreceptor tuned to the sulfur and ammonia that leak from Vesh’s cliff vents, and also to the faint metallic scent of others of its kind.

The head, if you insist on calling it that, is a blunt prow with a single horizontal slit. The slit is not a mouth and not an eye. It is both, and neither. Light enters; dissolved minerals leave. Inside the slit, a curtain of cilia sorts what arrives. Edible dust is swallowed into the fluid body. Useless grit is spat sideways in a dry hiss. When the glasslung is alarmed, the slit seals and the whole prow clouds over, turning from glass to milk in under a second. That clouding is a signal. Other glasslungs on the same cliff will cloud in answer, a ripple of opacity moving across the rock face like weather.

They do not hunt and they do not herd. They farm the wind. Every few hours a glasslung anchors, opens its fans wide, and lets the dusk-gale comb through them. Spores, ash, and the shed scales of smaller cliff-life stick to a sweet film the fans secrete. The creature then folds, rolls the film inward, and digests at leisure while the mineral grains in its body clink softly against one another. That clinking is the closest thing they have to a voice. Pitch changes with which grains are moving. Neighbors answer with their own arrangements of iron and silica. A listener who stayed long enough might learn that a high, bright rattle means a rich sporefall up-cliff, and a slow, heavy knock means the frost is creeping closer than it should.

Reproduction is a weather event. When the copper light dims under a dust pall and the air pressure drops, two or three glasslungs press their prows together until the slits align. Fluid passes both ways. Somewhere in the mixing, a knot of tissue pinches off, drops to the rock, and lies still for days, clouded and inert, while the adults resume their climbing. The knot thickens its walls, sorts its first grains from the dust, and eventually unfurls a pair of stubby fans. It does not follow its parents. The cliff is the parent. The wind is the parent. The adults have already forgotten the knot, except as a new pattern of clinks somewhere below.

If you stood near one at the right hour, you would see your own reflection slide across its flank, warped by the pulse underneath, and then watch that reflection cloud to milk as the creature decided you were only another change in the wind.
